titulo: Five vowels, one punch per word
subtitulo: Why the words you already recognise are the ones nobody understands — and the hand that fixes it

steps.pt: Welcome to Dime. I'm Alice, and I'm going to be honest with you from the first minute: Spanish pronunciation is not hard. It's just different in five small ways, and English speakers get all five wrong at once. Here's the strange part — the word you'll mangle worst is the word you already know. 'Hospital'. 'Chocolate'. 'Gracias'. You recognise them, so you don't slow down, and out comes something a Spanish barman genuinely cannot parse. So here's our deal, and it's a modest one: the right vowels in the fifty phrases that get you through the trip. Not sounding Spanish by September. Now put your hand flat on your leg, palm down. It's about to become your teacher. Spanish has five vowels — five, not twelve — and each one is a single, flat, unmoving sound. Ah. Eh. Ee. Oh. Oo. English vowels slide: 'no' comes out 'nooow', 'café' comes out 'ca-fay'. Spanish ones don't move. Keep the palm flat while you say each one — if your hand tilts, your vowel slid.
The whole vowel system. Hold each one for two seconds — if it slides inside the hold, it was a diphthong.
No, thanks. — Listen to that 'no'. It's one flat 'oh' and then it stops. Not 'noooow'.

steps.promptPt: The waiter is topping up your glass and you've had plenty. Turn him down — politely, two words, flat palm. Speak now.
steps.pt: No, thanks.

Second habit, and it's the one that makes you sound foreign even when every sound is right: rhythm. English is a drum kit — LOUD, quiet, LOUD, quiet, and the quiet bits collapse into a mumble. Spanish is a typewriter: every key hits the paper just as hard. So swap the hand over. Side of the hand, tapping your leg, one tap per syllable, every tap the same size. Bar-ce-lo-na — four taps, four equal taps, not 'Barsuh-LOH-nuh'. And here's the mistake everyone makes on their first go: don't tap the loud bit. Tap every bit. Every vowel gets paid; no syllable works for free.
Thank you very much. — Four beats, all the same size. Not 'MUCH-us GRASH-us'.

steps.promptPt: Someone has just picked up the glove you dropped in the street. Thank them properly — four equal taps on your leg as you say it. Speak now.
steps.pt: Thank you very much.

Guiri alert. 'Guiri' is what the Spanish call pink northern tourists like us — it's teasing, not an insult, and we've earned it. Here's how we give ourselves away. Listen to these, in glorious English: HOS-pi-tl. NATCH-rul. ANN-i-ml. CHOCK-lit. RES-tuh-ront. Every single one of those is also a Spanish word — and not one of them was understood. That's the o-tax: you recognise the word, so you hand it over with an English mouth and it vanishes. Rule of thumb, and it's the only one you need: a Spanish word you recognise is still a Spanish word. Same five vowels. Same one punch. This is the one moment in the whole course where all three habits run at once — equal taps, flat palm, one punch.
The same five words, handed back with a Spanish accent. Notice where the punch lands — it moved to the end.

Did you hear the punch move? English says HOS-pital. Spanish says os-pi-TAL. So here's the third gesture: one short punch in the air, once per word, on the loud syllable. And there's a rule that tells you where it goes — twenty seconds, three lines, and you'll never guess again. One: if the word ends in a vowel, an N or an S, the punch is on the second-to-last syllable — CA-sa, CO-men. Two: if it ends in any other consonant, the punch is on the last one — os-pi-TAL, ciu-DAD. Three: if there's a little mark over a vowel, the mark wins, always. That mark isn't decoration, it's a loudspeaker. Wherever it sits, that's where the punch goes.
Where is the hospital? — hear where the punch lands: right at the end, os-pi-TAL. And 'está' has the mark, so the mark wins.

steps.promptPt: You've cut your hand and the pharmacy has sent you on. Stop someone in the street and ask where the hospital is — and put the punch at the end, os-pi-TAL. Speak now.
steps.pt: Where is the hospital?

Now some good news, and it's free. Spain has a sound that Latin America doesn't, and English speakers already own it. The C in 'gracias', the Z in 'cerveza' — that is the 'th' in 'think'. You've been making that sound since you were three. Get it right and on your very first word you sound like someone who did the homework. It's a gift, not a test — nobody in Spain will blink if you say 'grasias', because half the Spanish-speaking world does. But do try it. One warning before you get carried away, because there's a predictable way to overdo this: 'gracias' is gra-th-ias, not gra-th-ia-th. The C is the 'th'. The final S stays an S. That's the whole rule. Overcook it and you're not doing Madrid, you're doing a broad Cádiz accent — which is a real and lovely accent, but on you it just sounds like a lisp.
👂 'That's fifty cents.' — You don't need to say this one. You need to survive hearing it. Four of the numbers on every bar bill carry that 'th': cinco, doce, quince, cincuenta.

The R. Fourth gesture: a quick flick of your finger, like flicking a crumb off the table — that's a single R, one tap of the tongue and gone. And you already make it. Americans: say 'butter'. That middle sound, the one that isn't really a T — that IS the Spanish R. Brits: say 'pot o' tea' fast, or do your worst Scottish accent on the word 'very'. Same thing. Now, the double R — 'perro', 'arroz' — is the rolled one, and I'm going to let you off it right now. Loose tongue, more air, don't try to make it happen, let the air do it. Practise on 'brrr, it's cold'. And if it comes out as a single flick and you say 'pero' when you meant 'perro' — nobody in Spain is going to hand you a dog. Context does the work. An English R is a problem. A weak Spanish R is not.
Excuse me, can I get a small draught beer? — Two flicks in there: pe-R-dona, and no English R anywhere. And that Ñ is just the middle of 'onion'.

steps.promptPt: You've finally caught the barman's eye. Get his attention and ask for a small draught beer — flick the R, don't roll into it. Speak now.
steps.pt: Excuse me, can I get a small draught beer?

One sound left, and it's the only one in Spanish that English genuinely doesn't have: the J. Not the J of 'jam'. Breathe out as if you were fogging up a window, then add a scrape right at the back of the throat. Brits, you have this for free: it's the 'ch' in 'loch'. Loch Ness. Americans, your nearest thing is 'Bach' — the composer, properly pronounced, not 'Bock' — or the 'ch' in 'Chanukah'. If neither lands, think of a hard H with a scrape behind it. Why bother? Because that sound is in 'jamón', 'ajo' — garlic — 'equipaje', 'Rioja' and 'naranja'. It is the consonant of food and luggage. Order 'ham-ON' with an English J and you'll get a smile. Order it with the loch and you'll get service.
Has it got ham in it? — two beats, the loch at the front of jamón and the punch on the last syllable.

steps.promptPt: A plate of green beans has arrived and in Spain there is very often ham hiding in them. Ask whether it's got ham in it — with the loch. Speak now.
steps.pt: Has it got ham in it?
Say it with him. Four equal taps, and the 'th'.

Sounds in focus, ninety seconds, then you're done. Everything you've just built runs off one hand: equal taps for rhythm, flat palm for vowels, one punch per word, one flick for the R. And the stress rule again, because it's the cheapest win in the course — vowel, N or S at the end, punch the second-to-last syllable; any other consonant, punch the last; and if there's an accent mark, the mark wins. Watch out for that mark, by the way: 'papá' is dad and 'papa' is potato, so the man who told the waiter his potato was waiting for him got exactly what he deserved. And the floor of this whole course, if you take nothing else from today: keep the vowels short, flat and equal. That one habit does more for being understood than the next fifty phrases. You will still sound foreign. Everyone will love you for trying.

That's part 1A. Five pure vowels, equal beats, one punch, a flicked R, a scraped J, and a free 'th' that marks you out as someone who came to Spain rather than to Mexico. Next, part 1B: walking into a bar and actually getting served — which in Spain has almost nothing to do with waiting politely. See you there.
See you later. — Four flat vowels, four equal beats. You already know how to say it.

secoes.titulo: The pronunciation respelling used in this app
secoes.corpo: Everything written in the grey line under the Spanish is aimed at an English-reading eye. ah, eh, ee, oh, oo are the five vowels — as in father, bed, see (short), or (without the r), boot. 'th' is the C before e/i and the Z — as in think, never as in this. 'dh' is the softened D between vowels — as in mother. 'kh' is the J and the G before e/i — as in Scottish loch. 'ny' is the Ñ — as in canyon. 'y' is LL and Y — as in yes, never the 'zh' of measure (that's Buenos Aires, not Madrid). 'r' is one tap; 'rr' is two or three. B and V are the same sound in Spain — there is no V. H is always silent. CAPITALS mark the stressed syllable.

exemplos.pt: GRAH-thyahs — the C is a 'th', the final S is an S
khah-MOHN — the loch, then the punch on the last syllable

secoes.corpo: 1. Word ends in a vowel, N or S → stress the second-to-last syllable: CA-sa, CO-men, gra-CIAS. 2. Word ends in any other consonant → stress the last syllable: hos-pi-TAL, ciu-DAD, es-pa-ÑOL. 3. There's a written accent → the accent overrides both rules, always: te-LÉ-fo-no, po-li-CÍ-a, ca-FÉ. The accent mark also separates pairs that mean very different things, and this is where it costs you something real.

secoes.titulo: Two more free gifts: Ñ and the soft D
secoes.corpo: The Ñ is not two sounds, it's one, and you already own it: it's the middle of 'onion'. In fact 'canyon' is the Spanish 'cañón', borrowed — that's etymology, not analogy. Say España in three beats with the Ñ inside the middle beat. Separately: a D between two vowels goes soft, all the way to the 'th' of 'father'. So 'nada' is closer to NAH-tha than NAH-da, and 'Madrid' ends in a whisper. And remember there is no V in Spain: 'vino' starts with a B.

exemplos.pt: noh PAH-sah NAH-dhah — 'no harm done', the most useful throwaway line in Spain

secoes.titulo: The rhythm argument, for the curious
secoes.corpo: The classic description separates syllable-timed languages (Spanish) from stress-timed ones (English). Modern phonetics argues about how strictly that holds and prefers measuring variability instead. None of that matters to you in a bar. What matters is the behaviour: in Spanish every syllable gets paid in full, and English speakers habitually short-change the unstressed ones into a schwa. Tap them all the same size and you have bought yourself the single biggest gain available.

secoes.titulo: The quiet false friends (read, don't drill)
secoes.corpo: These are the ones that cost you dignity rather than money, so they live here in text rather than in your ear. 'Largo' is long, not large. 'Ropa' is clothes, not rope. 'Carpeta' is a folder, not a carpet. 'Pie' is a foot. 'Sensible' means sensitive. 'Actualmente' means currently. 'Red' is a network — 'la red wifi'. 'Introducir' means to insert, which is why the cash machine tells you to 'introduzca su tarjeta'. And 'envolver' means to gift-wrap, so when the shop assistant asks '¿se lo envuelvo?', she is not involving you in anything.

exemplos.pt: Shall I wrap it for you? (shop)

permissao: You are allowed to sound foreign. Say 'grasias' with a plain S and nobody will blink, because most of the Spanish-speaking world says it that way. Let the double R come out as one flick — nobody is going to hand you a dog. Five flat vowels and one punch per word is the whole ask on day one; the 'th', the flick and the loch are bonuses you can collect any time before you fly.
espelho: Swallowing the quiet halves of your own words is the bit that reads as odd there. It does not arrive as a relaxed accent — it arrives as somebody talking with his mouth half closed, and the person in front of you keeps waiting for the end of a sentence you already finished.
frasePiso: Five flat vowels and one punch per word, and the fifty phrases you have not learned yet will land when you get to them. Most people who spend a fortnight in Spain never find out that this was the whole problem.

fichasCulturais.sinal: You say a word you both own — hospital, natural, chocolate — and the face in front of you goes blank for a second and then asks you to say it again.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: He did not hear me. Or my Spanish is so bad that even the easy words fail.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: The word is his too, and it arrived with English vowels and the punch on the wrong syllable, so it landed as a word he does not have. Recognising the word is exactly what makes you speed up, and speeding up is what breaks it — the part calls it the o-tax (docs/pesquisa-espanha.md §3, GUIRI ALERT).
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Say it again, slower, five flat vowels, one punch on the last syllable: os-pi-TAL.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: The words you already recognise — and there are hundreds of them — stop being the ones that fail, and you get served on the first go instead of the third.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not at a hotel desk or a tourist office, where the person opposite decodes English vowels all day and will get you first time. The tax is charged where nobody is paid to decode you: the bar, the market, the ticket window.

fatosDatados.afirmacao: Turning the final S of 'gracias' into a 'th' as well is not Madrid — it is a Cádiz accent, and on an English mouth it reads as a lisp.
